name: Violet Ultramarine
lede: Violet ultramarine, better known as ultramarine violet, is a blue-violet pigment made by chemically altering ultramarine blue.

sections.title: Two names, one pigment
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium treats violet ultramarine as a plain synonym for ultramarine violet and sends readers to that entry [1]. Several derivatives can be made from ultramarine by swapping its constituent elements, and this is one of them [1]. The same family gives ultramarine red [1].

The swatch is a deep blue-violet, close to [[indigo]] in hue but lighter and more purple, and a cooler neighbor of [[purple]] and [[blue-violet]].

sections.title: How it is made
sections.body:
The recipe starts with finished ultramarine blue. It is mixed with about 2.5 to 5 per cent ammonium chloride, heated to 200-250 degrees Celsius for four days, and exposed to air until the purple color develops [1]. An alternative route heats ultramarine with chlorine and hydrochloric acid [1]. The Colour Index lists it as Pigment Violet 15 [1].

In the painter's catalogue it sits in a short list of violets. Jarman names cobalt violet, [[manganese-violet]], ultramarine violet and Mars violet as the artist's violets, and calls violet the luxury among colors [2]. He also remarks that violet paint is rarely used, and that violet has the shortest wavelength of the spectrum, with the invisible ultraviolet behind it [2].

sections.title: Not to be confused with
sections.body: The Compendium also records that Mayer used the name violet ultramarine for alizarin violet, a pigment produced from synthetic purpurin in the way an alizarin lake is made [3]. Books disagree about which pigment the name points to, so check the maker's label: the ultramarine-based one is Pigment Violet 15 [1][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This color is almost absent from painting in our archive: 1 of 23,781 paintings holds it at all, and only as 10.8 per cent of one canvas, Sargent's *Bedouins* from 1905, in its shadows [4][[painting:commons-Q131754092|Bedouins]]. A single painting is not a trend [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a color on a screen, not a pigment test [4].
